lines.text: Back at the board. Name any opening to walk through it, or say what to sharpen.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to e 5 if it's still legal.
This game is the King's Pawn Game.

Their e5 stakes a claim in the center and opens lines for the pieces. The rule behind e4: stake out the center and grab space with the pawn to e4, because pieces behind a strong center reach either wing in a move or two. Their knight is still on g8, so nothing hits your pawn on e4 yet — it doesn't need a guard; development comes first.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to c 6 if it's still legal.
It's the Vienna Game: Max Lange Defense.
Their knight bears down on d4, holding back your d-pawn. The knight bears down on d5, holding back their d-pawn.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to b 6 if it's still legal.

They play b6 first, to free their bishop on c8 for bishop to b7. That move does the job here — it develops into the game, fighting for the center on d5, holding back the pawn on d7, eyeing e6 — f7 sits right beside their king. Keep your options open — the pawn move will still be there later, and a pawn move can't be taken back. Their bishop is still on c8, so nothing hits your bishop on c4 yet — it doesn't need a guard; development comes first.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to f 6 if it's still legal.

This is the Vienna Game: Stanley Variation, Three Knights Variation with your d3 and their b6 thrown in. Their knight bears down on d5, backing their d-pawn's push there, and e4, attacking your pawn there. c2, d3 and e4 form a chain: c2 is its base, the one pawn no other pawn guards, so that is the pawn to look after.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to c 5 if it's still legal.

They play bishop to c5 first, so they can castle next — a king left in the middle gets caught the moment the center opens. Their knight on c6 is tied down now: you hit the pawn on e5 once and it is guarded once — the knight is the guard that holds it. That is what pressure buys — a piece that cannot leave. Their bishop bears down on d4, holding back your d-pawn, and e3, a square no pawn of yours can cover.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight takes e 5 if it's still legal.

Their knight takes e5 does two jobs: it stops your e-pawn takes f6, and it prepares c6. Anything else, like bishop takes g1, gives up about two points. Their knight bears down on c4, attacking your bishop there, and d3, attacking your pawn there. Watch f2 — a knight lands there in 2 and forks your queen on d1 and rook on h1, so take the square away before it arrives.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to b 7 if it's still legal.

Bishop to b3 — now d5 doesn't work: you cover d5 three times to their two. Anything else, like bishop to b5, gives up about a point. Their bishop takes aim along the long diagonal. Your bishop leaves c4, so their knight can no longer take it there and double your pawns.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to b 4 if it's still legal.

Watch out — their bishop on b4 pins your knight on c3 against your king on e1. Remember — a pin freezes the piece in front: it can't move without exposing the more valuable piece behind it, so it can be piled on. Your knight on c3 cannot move at all — the king on e1 is behind it. Their knight has nothing defending it — find it, and taking it costs you nothing back. Before you take, check what taking it allows.
Look for the forcing move first — it beats the quiet one here.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight to c 6 if it's still legal.

Checks, captures, threats — there was a forcing move here, and this quiet move lets it go. Here's how: run CCT first — checks, captures, threats, in that order. Only when none of them works do you look at quiet moves — that order is what finds shots. You've walked into this before — missing a forcing move, the 8th game now — the last one was against nickpav018 over a year ago. Bishop to d2 was a blunder — it cost about two points of advantage. They answer bishop takes c3.
Now, you’d love to play the natural move with the knight to d5 — but they answer the bishop takes d2 and it falls apart.
Got it — after your move, they play Knight takes d 4 if it's still legal.
Their knight is guarded, but a cheaper piece of yours hits it — a guard does not save it.

After their knight taking on d4, you're at a fork in the road: one move keeps your edge. Take the extra minute. That was the move here — it attacks the knight on f6. Heads up: their bishop on b4 looks through your knight on c3 at your bishop on d2 and your king behind it — move the knight and the bishop is pinned.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop takes g 2 if it's still legal.
This loses the game if you ignore it — your rook on h1 is attacked and nothing's defending it.

Their bishop takes g2 is a blunder — it throws away about two points of advantage. Queen takes f6 was their move — it would walk the queen on d8 round to g6, by way of f6. There is something here for you now — look for it. That is the move this position asks for — it wins the knight on f6. Bishop to g5? That drops the rook on h1. Bishop to d5? That drops the rook on h1. After their bishop taking on g2, one move keeps the win, and only one. Worth thinking it through.
Got it — after your move, they play Queen takes f 6 if it's still legal.

This move hands them a tactic: they play knight takes b3 and, four moves later, you play rook takes g2, and it wins them a rook for a pawn. You've walked into this before — walking into a tactic, the third game now — the last one was against vribak about a month ago. G-knight to e2 was a blunder — it cost three or four points of advantage. They answer knight takes b3.
Your rook on h1 is still hanging — nothing guards it yet.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop takes h 1 if it's still legal.
They are hitting your knight on d4, and nothing guards it — it is lost unless it moves or gets a guard.

Your knight on d4 is attacked — but you don't have to move it or guard it; look for the move that makes taking it fail. You found it — it takes their knight on d4. Their bishop takes h1 is a mistake — it throws away more than a point of advantage. Queen to h4 with check was their move — it would land a fork. That tips the game your way — look for the move that keeps it.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to e 7 if it's still legal.
Threat met. Queen to e2 with check keeps your knight on d4 safe.
Your knight on d4 is still hanging — nothing guards it yet.

Their bishop to e7 is a mistake — it throws away more than a point of advantage. Queen to e7 was their move — it would line up an x-ray at your king on e1. That move does the job here — it takes the open e-file. Their bishop bears down on c5, backing their c-pawn's push there. Before the king moves, count the checks it walks into on each square. The plan changes here: their passed pawn on f7 is the danger — get a piece in front of it and blockade before it runs.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to b 7 if it's still legal.
You have a pin: your queen on e2 pins their bishop on e7 against their king on e8. The bishop on e7 is frozen: moving it would leave the king on e8 in check, which is illegal.

D-knight to b5? Then they play bishop to f3 and, three moves later, you play b-knight takes c7, check — you give up a rook for a pawn. That was the move here — it castles your king into safety and swings the rook toward the center. Castling gets your king to safety and brings the rook toward the center.
Got it — after your move, they play Castle queenside if it's still legal.
Both kings on the queenside: no pawn race — pushing the pawns in front of your own king only weakens it, so the fight is in the centre and on the other wing.

C-knight to b5? That drops the bishop on d5. Their king finds shelter on the queenside and the rook swings toward the open center. Of the two plans on offer, the stronger is getting the knight to a7, to take the pawn there; the f-file falls short by about a point.
Got it — after your move, they play King takes b 7 if it's still legal.
The check is a one-move idea; the plan is a quiet move that covers d4, keeping their queen off it.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to c 6 if it's still legal.

The bishop on d2 loses its diagonal to e4; keep your own pieces breathing. Here's how: before you park a queen in front of your own bishop, ask which diagonal it shuts. Develop the bishop first, or put the queen where the bishop still sees past it.
Count before you take on c6: two attackers against three defenders. Not enough — start the trades there and you come out behind.
Got it — after your move, they play Queen to h 4 if it's still legal.

Watch out — your queen on e4 is the only defender of your knight on d5 — and it can be taken. Remember — removing the guard takes away the piece defending a key square, and what it protected falls. It is attacked once and nothing guards it: queen takes e4 — they win a queen.

They left their bishop on e7 and hit your queen on e4 instead — the bigger threat comes first. That's danger levels: answer a threat with a threat to something worth more. Take the bishop with knight takes e7, and queen takes e4 takes your queen. There is something to collect, but your queen on e4 is loose and under fire — safety first — the material is not going anywhere.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop to c 5 if it's still legal.

Careful — this costs material if you ignore it: their pawn on c6 hits your knight on d5, and a guard does not help: the pawn is worth less than your knight. C-pawn takes d5 wins your knight for their pawn, even after you take back.

Knight to f5? Then they play queen to g4 and, two moves later, you play queen takes d5, check — you give up a knight for a pawn. Their bishop bears down on d4, attacking your knight there. Their queen on h4 pins your bishop on f4 to your queen on e4. Your pinned piece is a target — they can attack it again and it cannot run. g5 is the pile-on. Break the pin before it lands.
Got it — after your move, they play Pawn to f 5 if it's still legal.
b4 was a mistake — it let them play h-rook to e8, which attacks the queen on e4. The lasting concession: your king's pawn cover thinned (2 shield pawns down to 1).
Their bishop is guarded, but a cheaper piece of yours hits it — a guard does not save it.
Their f5 is a blunder — it throws away five points or more of advantage. H-rook to e8 was their move — it would attack the queen on e4.
Got it — after your move, they play Rook d to e 8 if it's still legal.
Your queen on e4 is still hanging — nothing guards it yet. Nothing guards one of their pieces — whatever takes it is not taken back.

You left your knight on d5 and went after their queen on h4 instead — the bigger threat comes first. That is the move this position asks for — it forks the queen on h4 and the pawn on g7. Your bishop on f4 is tied to guarding the pawn on h2 — but their queen on h4 is just as tied to attacking it, so the guard costs you nothing.
Got it — after your move, they play Queen to f 2 if it's still legal.
Watch out — this loses material if you ignore it: your knight on d5 is the only defender of your bishop on f4 — and it can be taken.

Their queen to f2 is imprecise. Queen to h5 was their move — it would walk the queen on h4 round to d1, by way of h5, and take the rook there. Their queen trains on the queen on g2 — pressure they have to answer. Your king's cover is thin — two of the pawns in front of it are gone and they already have pieces aimed at it. Look after the king before you throw more forces forward.
Got it — after your move, they play Bishop takes f 2 if it's still legal.

Their bishop takes f2 wins by force: you give up a queen for a rook — it is bishop takes f2 itself. Anything else, like h-rook to f8, gives up about a point. You found it — it takes their queen on f2.
Got it — after your move, they play King to a 8 if it's still legal.
Their rook is guarded, but a cheaper piece of yours hits it — a guard does not save it.

That's six in a row. Knight to d6 with check was the only move that kept the win. Now, you’d love to play the knight taking on b6 — but they take back and it falls apart. Their king steps toward safety; no place for it in the crossfire yet. Their king on a8 and rook on e8 now stand a knight's jump apart — that is the pattern to scan for: one square your knight can reach hits both.
Got it — after your move, they play King to b 8 if it's still legal.
They are hitting your knight on c7, and nothing guards it — it is lost unless it moves or gets a guard.

That move does the job here — it forks the king on a8 and the rook on e8. Knight to c7 with check brings your knight into the attack on their king — 2 of your pieces on it against 1 defender. Their king trains on the knight on c7 — pressure they have to answer. Your knight to c7 with check eyes a6, a square no pawn of theirs can cover.
